claim: Maternal exposure to di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) induces defects in spermatogenesis in successive generations in mice.
source: In mouse, maternal exposure to di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) is known to induce defects in spermatogenesis in successive generations, but the mechanism(s) of impaired spermatogenesis are unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing this phenomenon.

claim: Maternal DEHP exposure results in DNA hypermethylation of promoters of spermatogenesis-related genes in fetal testicular germ cells in F1 mice.
source: Here, we showed that maternal DEHP exposure results in DNA hypermethylation of promoters of spermatogenesis-related genes in fetal testicular germ cells in F1 mice
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RRBS analysis shown in the manuscript.

claim: Hypermethylation of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l persisted from fetal testicular cells to adult spermatogonia.
source: hypermethylation of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l, which are crucial for spermatogenesis, persisted from fetal testicular cells to adult spermatogonia
evidence: This claim is supported by RRBS and bisulfite sequencing data comparing E19.5 germ cells and adult spermatogonia.

claim: Hypermethylation of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l results in downregulation of expression of these genes.
source: hypermethylation of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l, which are crucial for spermatogenesis, persisted from fetal testicular cells to adult spermatogonia, resulting in the downregulation of expression of these genes
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data showing decreased expression in DEHP-exposed spermatogonia.

claim: Forced methylation of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l gene promoters silenced expression of these loci in a reporter assay.
source: Forced methylation of these gene promoters silenced expression of these loci in a reporter assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Maternal DEHP exposure-induced hypermethylation of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l results in downregulation of these genes in spermatogonia and subsequent defects in spermatogenesis, at least in the F1 generation.
source: These results suggested that maternal DEHP exposure-induced hypermethylation of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l results in downregulation of these genes in spermatogonia and subsequent defects in spermatogenesis, at least in the F1 generation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data on methylation, expression, and spermatogenic defects.

claim: Poor maternal nutrition during pregnancy was associated with low birth weight and greater risk of metabolic and cardiovascular diseases in offspring in the Dutch famine of 1944.
source: Historically, studies on the Dutch famine of 1944 indicated that poor maternal nutrition during pregnancy was associated with low birth weight as well as a greater risk of metabolic and cardiovascular diseases in offspring (Painter et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Painter et al., 2005.

claim: Maternal nutritional conditions resulted in changes in offspring DNA methylation patterns in the promoters of genes related to metabolic diseases and cardiac diseases.
source: Those studies also showed that maternal nutritional conditions resulted in changes in offspring in DNA methylation patterns in the promoters of genes related to metabolic diseases and cardiac diseases (Tobi et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tobi et al., 2009.

claim: Maternal nutritional change induced increased DNA methylation of CpG sites in the Avy allele and inhibition of expression of the corresponding gene in a rodent model.
source: In a rodent model, a maternal nutritional change induced increased DNA methylation of CpG sites in the Avy allele and inhibition of expression of the corresponding gene, which in turn may result in changes in the hair color of offspring (Waterland and Jirtle, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Waterland and Jirtle, 2003.

claim: Chemically induced liver damage influences paternally inherited suppressive adaptation for liver fibrosis in F1 and F2 generations mediated by epigenetic changes in sperm.
source: Specifically, chemically induced liver damage has been shown to influence paternally inherited suppressive adaptation for liver fibrosis in F1 and F2 generations; these effects are mediated by epigenetic changes in sperm, and up- and downregulation of anti- and pro-fibrogenic genes, respectively, in offspring (Zeybel et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zeybel et al., 2012.

claim: Paternal prediabetes alters DNA methylation of sperm genes encoding components of the insulin signaling pathway, leading to glucose intolerance and insulin resistance in offspring.
source: Concerning nutritional influences, paternal prediabetes has been shown to alter DNA methylation of sperm genes encoding components of the insulin signaling pathway, leading to glucose intolerance and insulin resistance in the offspring (Wei et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wei et al., 2014.

claim: Offspring of males fed a low-protein diet exhibit upregulation of genes involved in lipid and cholesterol biosynthesis and decreased levels of cholesterol esters in the liver.
source: Another example is that offspring of males fed a low-protein diet (LPD) exhibit upregulation of genes involved in lipid and cholesterol biosynthesis and decreased levels of cholesterol esters in the liver; these offspring also exhibit changes in the DNA methylation of genes involved in the regulation of lipid metabolism (Carone et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Carone et al., 2010.

claim: LPD-induced epigenetic changes in testicular germ cells are mediated by cyclic AMP-dependent transcription factor 7 (ATF7), with resulting effects on gene expression in offspring.
source: In addition, LPD-induced epigenetic changes (such as histone H3 lysine [K] 9 methylation levels and small RNA expression) in testicular germ cells have been shown to be mediated by cyclic AMP-dependent transcription factor 7 (ATF7), with resulting effects on gene expression in offspring (Yoshida et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yoshida et al., 2020.

claim: Aging results in DNA methylation changes of specific genes including neuronal development-related genes in sperm.
source: Aging also results in DNA methylation changes of specific genes including neuronal development-related genes in sperm (Yoshizaki et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yoshizaki et al., 2021.

claim: Heat shock or osmotic stress in adult or embryonic Drosophila induces phosphorylation of dATF-2 and results in the release of this protein from heterochromatin, which is transmitted to the next generation in a non-Mendelian fashion.
source: Heat shock or osmotic stress in adult or embryonic Drosophila induces phosphorylation of Drosophila activating transcriptional factor-2 (dATF-2) and results in the release of this protein from heterochromatin; this heterochromatic disruption is an epigenetic event that is transmitted to the next generation in a non-Mendelian fashion (Seong et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Seong et al., 2011.

claim: Starvation-induced developmental arrest in C. elegans leads to production of small RNAs that are inherited through at least three consecutive generations and target genes with roles in nutrition.
source: In C. elegans, starvation-induced developmental arrest leads to production of small RNAs that are inherited through at least three consecutive generations; these small RNAs target genes with roles in nutrition (Rechavi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rechavi et al., 2014.

claim: Transgenerational defects in spermatogenesis have been demonstrated in rodents after maternal exposure to vinclozolin.
source: Transgenerational defects in spermatogenesis have been demonstrated in rodents after maternal exposure to several chemicals, including vinclozolin (Anway et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Anway et al., 2005.

claim: Transgenerational defects in spermatogenesis have been demonstrated in rodents after maternal exposure to arsenic.
source: Transgenerational defects in spermatogenesis have been demonstrated in rodents after maternal exposure to several chemicals, including vinclozolin (Anway et al., 2005), arsenic (Yin et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yin et al., 2021.

claim: Transgenerational defects in spermatogenesis have been demonstrated in rodents after maternal exposure to p,p′-DDE.
source: Transgenerational defects in spermatogenesis have been demonstrated in rodents after maternal exposure to several chemicals, including vinclozolin (Anway et al., 2005), arsenic (Yin et al., 2021), and p,p′-dichlorodiphenoxydichloroethylene (p,p′-DDE), one of the primary metabolic products of the classical organochlorine pesticide, dichlorodiphenoxytrichloroethane (DDT) (Song et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Song et al., 2014.

claim: Changes of DNA methylation in fetal germ cells and spermatogenetic cells in postnatal testis occur after prenatal exposure to vinclozolin.
source: Recent work has demonstrated changes of DNA methylation in fetal germ cells and spermatogenetic cells in postnatal testis after prenatal exposure to vinclozolin (Skinner et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Skinner et al., 2019.

claim: Changes of DNA methylation in fetal germ cells and spermatogenetic cells in postnatal testis occur after prenatal exposure to DDT.
source: Recent work has demonstrated changes of DNA methylation in fetal germ cells and spermatogenetic cells in postnatal testis after prenatal exposure to vinclozolin (Skinner et al., 2019) and DDT (Ben Maamar et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ben Maamar et al., 2019.

claim: A causal relationship between altered DNA methylation/gene expression and spermatogenetic defects after prenatal exposure to vinclozolin or DDT has not been determined.
source: Recent work has demonstrated changes of DNA methylation in fetal germ cells and spermatogenetic cells in postnatal testis after prenatal exposure to vinclozolin (Skinner et al., 2019) and DDT (Ben Maamar et al., 2019), but a causal relationship between the altered DNA methylation/gene expression and the spermatogenetic defects has not been determined.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of evidence in cited literature.

claim: DEHP is a plasticizer used in a wide range of consumer products, such as food packing, medical devices, and wallpapers.
source: Di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) is a plasticizer that is used in a wide range of consumer products, such as food packing, medical devices, and wallpapers.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about DEHP.

claim: Maternal exposure to DEHP affects spermatogenesis in male offspring of mouse.
source: Maternal exposure to DEHP has been shown to affect spermatogenesis in male offspring of mouse (Doyle et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Doyle et al., 2013.

claim: Maternal exposure to DEHP affects the female reproductive system over multiple generations.
source: Maternal exposure to DEHP has been shown to affect spermatogenesis in male offspring of mouse (Doyle et al., 2013) as well as several other body systems over multiple generations, including the female reproductive system (Brehm et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brehm et al., 2018.

claim: Maternal exposure to DEHP affects the liver over multiple generations.
source: Maternal exposure to DEHP has been shown to affect spermatogenesis in male offspring of mouse (Doyle et al., 2013) as well as several other body systems over multiple generations, including the female reproductive system (Brehm et al., 2018), liver (Wen et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wen et al., 2020.

claim: Maternal exposure to DEHP affects anxiety-like behavior over multiple generations.
source: Maternal exposure to DEHP has been shown to affect spermatogenesis in male offspring of mouse (Doyle et al., 2013) as well as several other body systems over multiple generations, including the female reproductive system (Brehm et al., 2018), liver (Wen et al., 2020), and anxiety-like behavior (Quinnies et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Quinnies et al., 2015.

claim: Offspring exposed prenatally to DEHP show defects in spermatogenesis, decreases in sperm number, and reduction of sperm motility.
source: Concerning influences on spermatogenic cells, offspring that are exposed prenatally to DEHP show defects in spermatogenesis, decreases in sperm number, and reduction of sperm motility (Doyle et al., 2013; Prados et al., 2015; Stenz et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Doyle et al., 2013; Prados et al., 2015; Stenz et al., 2017.

claim: F1 sperm demonstrate altered DNA methylation and expression of genes encoding Svs2, Svs3b, Svs4, and Sva after prenatal DEHP exposure.
source: F1 sperm demonstrate altered DNA methylation and expression of the genes encoding seminal vesicle secretory protein 2 (Svs2; also known as semenogelin-1); Svs3b; Svs4; and seminal vesicle antigen (Sva), all of which are involved in sperm motility (Stenz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stenz et al., 2017.

claim: Testicular abnormalities including vacuoles in tubules (Type A), no lumen in tubules (Type B), and tubules containing apoptotic cells (Type C) were observed in F1 males of the DEHP group.
source: Testicular abnormalities, including vacuoles in tubules (Type A), no lumen in tubules (Type B), and tubules containing apoptotic cells detected as active caspase-3 immunoreactive cells in addition to by histological examination (Type C), were observed in F1 males of the DEHP group, while few abnormal tubules were found in the oil group as vehicle control (Figure 1A), as previously reported (Doyle et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1A and citation to Doyle et al., 2013.

claim: F2 males of the DEHP group showed similar histological abnormalities to F1 males.
source: F2 males of the DEHP group showed similar histological abnormalities (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The ratio of abnormal tubules in DEHP-exposed F1 testes was six-fold higher compared to oil-exposed F1 testes.
source: Quantitative evaluation of the abnormal testicular tubules showed six- and twofold increases of the ratios of the abnormal tubules in the DEHP-exposed F1 and F2 testes, respectively, compared with those in the oil-exposed groups (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The ratio of abnormal tubules in DEHP-exposed F2 testes was two-fold higher compared to oil-exposed F2 testes.
source: Quantitative evaluation of the abnormal testicular tubules showed six- and twofold increases of the ratios of the abnormal tubules in the DEHP-exposed F1 and F2 testes, respectively, compared with those in the oil-exposed groups (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Type B abnormality was not observed in F2 testes.
source: Classification of the types of the abnormalities, as shown in Figure 1A, revealed that Type B was not observed in F2 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There is some difference in the nature of spermatogenic failure between F1 and F2 testes.
source: Classification of the types of the abnormalities, as shown in Figure 1A, revealed that Type B was not observed in F2 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—source data 1), suggesting some difference in the nature of spermatogenic failure between the F1 and the F2 testes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Type B abnormality was absent in F2.

claim: A significant increase in the number of multinucleated germ cells was observed in E19.5 testis in animals prenatally exposed to DEHP compared to oil-exposed animals.
source: In addition, a significant increase in the number of multinucleated germ cells was observed in embryonic day (E) 19.5 testis in animals prenatally exposed to DEHP compared with those in an oil-exposed group (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1), as reported previously (Ungewitter et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F and citation to Ungewitter et al., 2017.

claim: Methylation levels in CpG cytosines in various genomic features showed similar methylation levels between oil- and DEHP-exposed groups in each germ cell population.
source: Comparison of methylation levels in CpG cytosines in various genomic features (including promoters, gene bodies, CpG islands, CpG island shores, and transposons) showed similar methylation levels between the oil- and the DEHP-exposed groups in each germ cell population in all genomic regions (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RRBS data shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Promoters in spermatogonial DNA tended to be hypermethylated compared to those in other germ cell populations.
source: At the same time, the methylation profiles differed strikingly between spermatogonia and other germ cell populations, such that the promoters in spermatogonial DNA tended to be hypermethylated compared to those in other cell populations, a result that is consistent with the mean methylation levels shown in Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by heatmap analysis in Figure 3A and data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: 80 promoters (78 genes) showed hypermethylation in DEHP-exposed E19.5 germ cells compared to oil-exposed E19.5 germ cells.
source: This analysis identified 80 and 22 promoters (78 and 20 genes) with hyper- and hypomethylation, respectively, in DEHP groups (compared to oil groups; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RRBS data shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: 22 promoters (20 genes) showed hypomethylation in DEHP-exposed E19.5 germ cells compared to oil-exposed E19.5 germ cells.
source: This analysis identified 80 and 22 promoters (78 and 20 genes) with hyper- and hypomethylation, respectively, in DEHP groups (compared to oil groups; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RRBS data shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Spermatogenesis-related GO terms such as meiotic cell cycle and spermatogenesis were enriched in hypermethylated genes in E19.5 germ cells.
source: Functional enrichment analysis revealed that spermatogenesis-related gene ontology (GO) terms such as meiotic cell cycle and spermatogenesis were enriched in hypermethylated genes in germ cells, while such enrichment was not observed in hypermethylated genes in testicular somatic cells (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Spermatogenesis-related GO terms were not enriched in hypermethylated genes in E19.5 testicular somatic cells.
source: Functional enrichment analysis revealed that spermatogenesis-related gene ontology (GO) terms such as meiotic cell cycle and spermatogenesis were enriched in hypermethylated genes in germ cells, while such enrichment was not observed in hypermethylated genes in testicular somatic cells (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 191 promoter regions (182 genes) showed hypermethylation in DEHP-exposed F1 spermatogonia compared to oil-exposed F1 spermatogonia.
source: We also compared methylation in F1 adult testicular germ cells and identified 191, 43, and 2 promoter regions (182, 42, 2 genes) with hypermethylation in spermatogonia, spermatocytes, and round spermatids, respectively, in the DEHP group compared with those in the oil group
evidence: This claim is supported by RRBS data shown in Supplementary file 3.

claim: 43 promoter regions (42 genes) showed hypermethylation in DEHP-exposed F1 spermatocytes compared to oil-exposed F1 spermatocytes.
source: We also compared methylation in F1 adult testicular germ cells and identified 191, 43, and 2 promoter regions (182, 42, 2 genes) with hypermethylation in spermatogonia, spermatocytes, and round spermatids, respectively, in the DEHP group compared with those in the oil group
evidence: This claim is supported by RRBS data shown in Supplementary file 3.

claim: 2 promoter regions (2 genes) showed hypermethylation in DEHP-exposed F1 round spermatids compared to oil-exposed F1 round spermatids.
source: We also compared methylation in F1 adult testicular germ cells and identified 191, 43, and 2 promoter regions (182, 42, 2 genes) with hypermethylation in spermatogonia, spermatocytes, and round spermatids, respectively, in the DEHP group compared with those in the oil group
evidence: This claim is supported by RRBS data shown in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Spermatogenesis-related genes were enriched only in hypermethylated genes in F1 spermatogonia.
source: We also compared methylation in F1 adult testicular germ cells and identified 191, 43, and 2 promoter regions (182, 42, 2 genes) with hypermethylation in spermatogonia, spermatocytes, and round spermatids, respectively, in the DEHP group compared with those in the oil group, among which spermatogenesis-related genes were enriched only in spermatogonia (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 26 genes were hypermethylated in both E19.5 germ cells and F1 spermatogonia.
source: We found 26 genes that were hypermethylated in both E19.5 germ cells and F1 spermatogonia; of these 26 genes, 9 encoded products related to spermatogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 9 of the 26 genes hypermethylated in both E19.5 germ cells and F1 spermatogonia encoded products related to spermatogenesis.
source: We found 26 genes that were hypermethylated in both E19.5 germ cells and F1 spermatogonia; of these 26 genes, 9 encoded products related to spermatogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: No hypermethylated and spermatogenesis-related genes were found to be shared between E19.5 germ cells and spermatocytes or round spermatids.
source: Meanwhile, no hypermethylated and spermatogenesis-related genes were found to be shared between the E19.5 germ cells and spermatocytes or round spermatids (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: DEHP preferentially induced hypermethylation in spermatogenesis-related genes in fetal germ cells, which is maintained up to the spermatogonial stage in F1 testis.
source: These results implied that the DEHP preferentially induced hypermethylation in spermatogenesis-related genes in fetal germ cells, which is maintained up to the spermatogonial stage in F1 testis, though this methylome analysis has low statistical power to capture the reliable global differences of DNA methylation due to the small number of replicates.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that spermatogenesis-related genes were hypermethylated in both E19.5 germ cells and F1 spermatogonia.

claim: The expression of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l was significantly decreased in DEHP-exposed F1 spermatogonia compared to oil-exposed F1 spermatogonia.
source: This assay showed that the expression of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l was significantly decreased in the DEHP group (compared to the oil group; Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Methylation of CpG sites in two regions in the Hist1h2ba promoter was significantly elevated in DEHP-exposed F1 spermatogonia compared to oil-exposed F1 spermatogonia.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, C, Figure 4—source data 1, methylation of the CpG sites in two regions in the Hist1h2ba promoter and one region in Sycp1 promoter was significantly elevated in DEHP-exposed spermatogonia (compared to the levels in the oil group).
evidence: This claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 4B, C.

claim: Methylation of CpG sites in one region in the Sycp1 promoter was significantly elevated in DEHP-exposed F1 spermatogonia compared to oil-exposed F1 spermatogonia.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, C, Figure 4—source data 1, methylation of the CpG sites in two regions in the Hist1h2ba promoter and one region in Sycp1 promoter was significantly elevated in DEHP-exposed spermatogonia (compared to the levels in the oil group).
evidence: This claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 4B, C.

claim: Taf7l in DEHP-exposed F1 spermatogonia tended to be hypermethylated, though this effect was not statistically significant.
source: Taf7l in DEHP-exposed spermatogonia also tended to be hypermethylated, though this effect was not statistically significant (Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Hypermethylation of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l in F1 spermatogonia following maternal DEHP exposure could contribute to the decreased expression of these genes, leading to spermatogenic abnormalities.
source: These results suggested that hypermethylation of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l in F1 spermatogonia following maternal DEHP exposure could contribute to the decreased expression of these genes, leading in turn to spermatogenic abnormalities.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined observations of hypermethylation, decreased expression, and spermatogenic abnormalities.

claim: Methylation levels of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l in F1 spermatogonia were decreased along with spermatogenesis.
source: However, none or few hypermethylated genes in E19.5 germ cells were shared between spermatocytes and round spermatids in F1 testis (Figure 3D), and methylation levels of the above-mentioned three spermatogenesis-related genes (Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l) in spermatogonia were decreased along with spermatogenesis (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by methylation data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The methylation level in the DEHP group was decreased more drastically than in the oil group during spermatogenesis, achieving levels similar to those observed in round spermatids in the oil group.
source: In addition, the methylation level in the DEHP group was decreased more drastically than was that in the oil group, achieving levels similar to those observed in round spermatids in the oil group.
evidence: This claim is supported by methylation data shown in Figure 5.

claim: F2 spermatogonia were not significantly altered in expression and methylation of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l.
source: We found that F2 spermatogonia were not significantly altered in these parameters, while they exhibited a weak and statistically not significant tendency to decreased expression of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l, and to hypermethylation of Hist1h2ba and Sycp1 in the DEHP-treated groups compared to the control groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR and bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Luc activity was significantly decreased by methylation of the promoter of Hist1h2ba.
source: We found that Luc activity was significantly decreased by methylation of the promoter of each gene (Figure 6B–D, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Luc activity was significantly decreased by methylation of the promoter of Sycp1.
source: We found that Luc activity was significantly decreased by methylation of the promoter of each gene (Figure 6B–D, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Luc activity was significantly decreased by methylation of the promoter of Taf7l.
source: We found that Luc activity was significantly decreased by methylation of the promoter of each gene (Figure 6B–D, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Hypermethylation of Hist1h2ba, Scyp1, and Taf7l results in decreased expression in testicular germ cells.
source: The results supported the hypothesis that hypermethylation of Hist1h2ba, Scyp1, and Taf7l results in decreased expression in testicular germ cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the luciferase reporter assay results.

claim: Induction of abnormal spermatogenesis in offspring following maternal DEHP exposure was first demonstrated using CD1 mice.
source: Induction of abnormal spermatogenesis in offspring following maternal DEHP exposure was first demonstrated using CD1 mice (Doyle et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Doyle et al., 2013.

claim: Abnormal spermatogenesis following maternal DEHP exposure was subsequently found in several strains of mice (including C57BL/6) and rats.
source: Induction of abnormal spermatogenesis in offspring following maternal DEHP exposure was first demonstrated using CD1 mice (Doyle et al., 2013) and subsequently was found in several strains of mice (including C57BL/6) and rats (Prados et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Prados et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015.

claim: The two histone variants HIST1H2AA and HIST1H2BA are abundant in the testis.
source: The two histone variants HIST1H2AA and HIST1H2BA are abundant in the testis (Trostle-Weige et al., 1982)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Trostle-Weige et al., 1982.

claim: Male mice lacking both Hist1h2aa and Hist1h2ba are sterile.
source: male mice lacking both Hist1h2aa and Hist1h2ba are sterile (Shinagawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shinagawa et al., 2015.

claim: Abnormal localization of nuclei in spermatids following maternal DEHP exposure is consistent with the phenotype observed in animals lacking both Hist1h2ba and Hist1h2aa.
source: Abnormal localization of nuclei in spermatids following maternal DEHP exposure (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1) is consistent with the phenotype observed in animals lacking both Hist1h2ba and Hist1h2aa, a phenotype that likely reflects impaired replacement of histones by protamine during spermiogenesis (Shinagawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of observed phenotypes with those reported in Shinagawa et al., 2015.

claim: The Hist1h2aa and Hist1h2ba genes are located tandemly in inverted orientation on chromosome 13 in mouse.
source: The Hist1h2aa and Hist1h2ba genes are located tandemly in inverted orientation on chromosome 13 in mouse (Figure 6)
evidence: This claim is based on established genomic knowledge and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Expression of Hist1h2aa and Hist1h2ba is controlled by a shared promoter located between the two genes.
source: expression of the two loci is controlled by a shared promoter located between the two genes (Huh et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Huh et al., 1991.

claim: There was a tendency toward reduced Hist1h2aa expression in addition to significant downregulation of Hist1h2ba expression following maternal DEHP exposure.
source: Consistent with that structure, we found a tendency toward reduced Hist1h2aa expression in addition to significant downregulation of Hist1h2ba expression (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1) following maternal DEHP exposure
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Hypermethylation of the shared promoter affects the expression of Hist1h2aa and Hist1h2ba in testicular germ cells.
source: suggesting that hypermethylation of the shared promoter affects the expression of these two genes in testicular germ cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that both genes showed reduced expression and share a promoter.

claim: SYCP1 is a component of the synaptonemal complex, a structure that connects homologous chromosomes in meiotic prophase.
source: SYCP1 is a component of the synaptonemal complex, a structure that connects homologous chromosomes in meiotic prophase
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about SYCP1 function.

claim: Sycp1 null mice are sterile because of spermatogenic arrest at the pachytene stage.
source: Sycp1 null mice are sterile because of spermatogenic arrest at the pachytene stage (de Vries, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Vries, 2005.

claim: Downregulation of Sycp1 expression is a cause of abnormal spermatogenesis following maternal DEHP exposure.
source: A similar abnormality was observed in F1 mice following maternal DEHP exposure (Figure 1A), a result that suggests that downregulation of Sycp1 expression is a cause of abnormal spermatogenesis following maternal DEHP exposure.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity of phenotypes between Sycp1 null mice and DEHP-exposed mice.

claim: TAF7L is a testis-specific transcription-associated factor.
source: TAF7L is a testis-specific transcription-associated factor (Pointud et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pointud et al., 2003.

claim: Taf7l null testis exhibits sperm with abnormal morphology and reduced motility, and large vacuoles are seen in the seminiferous tubules.
source: Taf7l null testis exhibits sperm with abnormal morphology and reduced motility, and large vacuoles are seen in the seminiferous tubules (Cheng et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cheng et al., 2007.

claim: The defects in Taf7l null testis resemble the abnormal tubules seen in the F1 testis following maternal DEHP exposure.
source: Taf7l null testis exhibits sperm with abnormal morphology and reduced motility, and large vacuoles are seen in the seminiferous tubules (Cheng et al., 2007); these defects resemble the abnormal tubules seen in the F1 testis following maternal DEHP exposure.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of phenotypes between Taf7l null mice and DEHP-exposed mice.

claim: The Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l genes are epi-mutated following maternal DEHP exposure.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that the Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l genes are epi-mutated following maternal DEHP exposure
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined observations of hypermethylation and downregulation of these genes.

claim: The downregulation of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l may be a cause of abnormal spermatogenesis following maternal DEHP exposure.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that the Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l genes are epi-mutated following maternal DEHP exposure; the resulting downregulation of these gene may be a cause of abnormal spermatogenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined observations of gene downregulation and spermatogenic defects.

claim: Maternal DEHP exposure induces DNA methylation not only in testis but also in other tissues such as adrenal gland and liver.
source: Previous studies have shown that maternal DEHP exposure induces DNA methylation not only in testis but also in other tissues such as adrenal gland and liver (Quinnies et al., 2015; Wen et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Quinnies et al., 2015; Wen et al., 2020.

claim: DEHP exposure resulted in a significant increase in the expression of Dnmt1 in the liver of the offspring.
source: notably, DEHP exposure resulted in a significant increase in the expression, in the liver of the offspring, of Dnmt1, a gene encoding a DNA methyltransferase.
evidence: This claim is based on prior studies cited in the discussion.

claim: Upregulation of Dnmt1 by DEHP plays a role in DNA hypermethylation.
source: These results suggested that upregulation of Dnmt1 by DEHP plays a role in DNA hypermethylation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from prior observations.

claim: MEHP, a hydrolyzed metabolite of DEHP, induces ROS production in adult testicular germ cells.
source: ROS may be involved in DEHP-induced DNA methylation, given that mono (2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (MEHP), a hydrolyzed metabolite of DEHP, induces ROS production in adult testicular germ cells (Kasahara et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kasahara et al., 2002.

claim: ROS directly enhances DNA methylation.
source: ROS may be involved in DEHP-induced DNA methylation, given that mono (2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (MEHP), a hydrolyzed metabolite of DEHP, induces ROS production in adult testicular germ cells (Kasahara et al., 2002), and that ROS directly enhances DNA methylation (Afanas'ev, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Afanas'ev, 2014.

claim: The chromatin structure around spermatogenesis-related genes is highly accessible in fetal germ cells.
source: In fetal germ cells, the chromatin structure around spermatogenesis-related genes is highly accessible (Li et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2018.

claim: Highly accessible chromatin structure may facilitate preferential DNA methylation of spermatogenesis-related genes in fetal germ cells in response to ROS accumulation following DEHP exposure.
source: In fetal germ cells, the chromatin structure around spermatogenesis-related genes is highly accessible (Li et al., 2018) and may facilitate preferential DNA methylation of spermatogenesis-related genes in fetal germ cells in response to the accumulation of ROS following DEHP exposure.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from chromatin accessibility and ROS effects.

claim: DEHP and MEHP are ligands of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) and the constitutive androstane receptor (CAR).
source: DEHP and MEHP are ligands of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) and the constitutive androstane receptor (CAR); these receptors regulate downstream pathways (Corton and Lapinskas, 2005; Eveillard et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Corton and Lapinskas, 2005; Eveillard et al., 2009.

claim: PPARs and CAR may promote DNA methylation via unknown mechanisms, including recruitment of DNA methylation-related molecules to target genes.
source: these receptors regulate downstream pathways (Corton and Lapinskas, 2005; Eveillard et al., 2009) and may thereby promote DNA methylation via unknown mechanisms, including recruitment of DNA methylation-related molecules to target genes.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism.

claim: Changes of the expression and methylation of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l in F2 spermatogonia were not statistically significant after maternal DEHP exposure.
source: Changes of the expression and methylation of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l in F2 spermatogonia were not statistically significant after maternal DEHP exposure (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Methylation levels in Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l in F2 spermatogonia generally were lower than those in F1 spermatogonia, even in the oil-treated group.
source: In our results, methylation levels in these genes in F2 spermatogonia generally were lower than those in F1 spermatogonia, even in the oil-treated group (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, C, Figure 4—source data 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of methylation data between F1 and F2.

claim: Differences in methylation levels between F1 and F2 spermatogonia may be due, at least in part, to differences in the purity of the spermatogonia.
source: these differences may be due, at least in part, to differences in the purity of the spermatogonia.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible explanation for observed differences.

claim: Enrichment of Gfra1 expression in sorted spermatogonia fractions was higher in F1 than in F2.
source: We found that enrichment of Gfra1 expression in sorted spermatogonia fractions was higher in those of F1 than those of F2, though its enrichment between oil- and DEHP-treated groups of F1 and of F2 was comparable (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The influence of DEHP-induced epigenetic changes may become weaker or disappear in the F2 alleles compared with those in the F1 alleles.
source: Because the F2 alleles are inherited from DEHP-exposed males and untreated females, the influence of DEHP-induced epigenetic changes reasonably may become weaker or disappear in the F2 alleles compared with those in the F1 alleles.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about inheritance patterns.

claim: The hypermethylation of Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l by DEHP is not directly transmitted to the F2.
source: Additionally, those genes became hypomethylated during spermatogenesis in F1 testis (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1), suggesting that the hypermethylation of the genes by DEHP is not directly transmitted to the F2.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that methylation decreases during spermatogenesis.

claim: Binding of transcription factors at CpG sites affects the methylation status of these sites during demethylation in primordial germ cells and affects subsequent re-methylation of these sites.
source: A recent study suggested that binding of transcription factors (TFs) at CpG sites affects the methylation status of these sites during demethylation in primordial germ cells and affects subsequent re-methylation of these sites; notably, CpG sites not bound by TFs could be re-methylated after demethylation (Kremsky and Corces, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kremsky and Corces, 2020.

claim: Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l are demethylated during spermatogenesis, and subsequently are re-methylated at some developmental time point(s) after fertilization.
source: These results imply that Hist1h2ba, Sycp1, and Taf7l are demethylated during spermatogenesis, and subsequently are re-methylated at some developmental time point(s) after fertilization.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of demethylation during spermatogenesis and the cited study on re-methylation.

claim: Abnormal DNA hypomethylation in F1 sperm due to embryonic undernutrition is not inherited in F2 sperm and somatic tissues.
source: In the case of embryonic undernutrition, abnormal DNA hypomethylation in F1 sperm is not inherited in F2 sperm and somatic tissues; however, the transcription levels of several genes near the regions with altered DNA methylation in F1 sperm are dysregulated in F2 somatic tissues (Radford et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Radford et al., 2014.

claim: Changes in DNA methylation perturb gene expression patterns in subsequent generations indirectly.
source: These results suggest that changes in DNA methylation perturb (indirectly) gene expression patterns in subsequent generations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited study on embryonic undernutrition.

claim: Modified histones that are bound to specific genomic regions, such as H3K4me3 bound at CpG-rich promoters and H3K9me3 bound at satellite repeats, are not replaced by protamine during sperm development.
source: Modified histones that are bound to specific genomic regions, such as H3K4 trimethylation (me3) bound at CpG-rich promoters and H3K9me3 bound at satellite repeats in the sperm genome, are not replaced by protamine during sperm development (Yamaguchi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yamaguchi et al., 2018.

claim: Maternal undernutrition and maternal DEHP exposure may affect histone modifications in F1 sperm in a DNA methylation status-dependent manner, which in turn may influence phenotypes in the F2.
source: Maternal undernutrition, as well as maternal DEHP exposure, may affect such histone modifications in F1 sperm in a DNA methylation status-dependent manner, which in turn may influence phenotypes in the F2.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a possible mechanism for transgenerational effects.
